card.h1: Student Authentication Portal: what happens between "Log in" and "Welcome, Priya"
A fast hash is a broken hash, which is why this lab starts at the database
card.p: The naive portal stores the password. The slightly-less-naive one stores SHA-256 of the password. Both fail, and the reason is speed.

ul.li: Speed is the attack. Fast hashes like SHA-256 let an attacker who steals the table make very large numbers of guesses quickly, so OWASP rules them out for passwords
Salt kills the lookup table. A unique per-user salt means two students who both chose "college@123" get two different stored values, so precomputed rainbow tables buy the attacker nothing
What OWASP actually prescribes: Argon2id first, minimum 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, parallelism 1. bcrypt is the legacy option at work factor 10 or more, with a 72-byte password limit
Our choice: bcrypt at cost 12, knowingly the legacy option, because it installs cleanly in a lab and its output string is readable enough to teach from on slide 4

card.h1: Three tiers, one trust boundary, and everything interesting happens at the middle one
card.p: No application code ships with this deck. What follows is the proposed reference implementation for the lab build, described exactly as we intend to write it.

ul.li: Client: HTML/CSS + fetch() with credentials: "include" so the session cookie rides along. Two forms and a profile page. It holds no authority and cannot read the token
API: Node.js + Express. Routers for /register, /login, /profile, /logout, plus the auth middleware that guards the protected one
Data: MongoDB + Mongoose. A Student model with roll number, email, and hash. The plaintext password is never a field, never logged, never returned
Libraries: bcryptjs for hashing, jsonwebtoken for signing, cookie-parser to read the cookie server-side, dotenv for the secret, express-rate-limit for the login door

card.h1: Registration: the stored string carries its own salt, cost, and algorithm
card.p: POST /api/auth/register. Validate, reject duplicates, hash, store. The demo moment is opening the database and reading the hash aloud.

ul.li: The code: const hash = await bcrypt.hash(req.body.password, 12) then await Student.create({ rollNo, email, hash })
Anatomy of the output $2b$12$Xy7...: 2b is the bcrypt variant, 12 is the cost, the next 22 characters are the salt, the remaining 31 are the digest. One 60-character field, so no separate salt column
Cost 12 means 2^12 key-setup rounds. The value is logarithmic, so raising it by one doubles the work
Returns 201 with the student's name and roll number. Never the hash, because a response body is a place data leaks from

card.h1: Login: compare, sign, and hand the token to the browser as a cookie it cannot read
card.p: bcrypt.compare re-hashes the submitted password with the salt it read out of the stored string, then compares. On success we sign a token and set it.

ul.li: Sign, then set: const token = jwt.sign({ sub: student._id, role: "student" }, process.env.JWT_SECRET, { expiresIn: "15m" }), then res.cookie("token", token, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "strict", maxAge: 900000 })

Two dots, three parts: header.payload.signature, each Base64Url-encoded, encoded and signed, not encrypted. Copy the cookie value out of DevTools, paste it into jwt.io, and the payload is plain JSON on screen. So no marks, no fees, no personal data in claims
The signature is the only thing doing work. It proves the server minted this token and nobody edited role:"student" into role:"admin"
One error message for both failures. Unknown email and wrong password both return 401 "Invalid credentials". Separate messages would let an attacker enumerate which roll numbers exist
Lab caveat: secure: true means the cookie only travels over HTTPS, so drive that flag from an environment variable and say so rather than quietly disabling it

card.h1: The middleware is the whole authorization story, in about twelve lines
card.p: GET /api/student/profile never sees an unverified request. The guard runs first, and it either attaches an identity or ends the request.

ul.li: Read: const token = req.cookies.token, available because cookie-parser ran first. No cookie, 401, done
Verify: jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET) checks the signature and the exp claim. Tampered or expired, 401. Pin the expected algorithm so alg: none is never accepted
Attach: set req.user = payload and call next(). Downstream handlers read identity from the verified token, never from the request body

The cookie's cost: the browser now sends the credential automatically, so state-changing routes need a CSRF token. SameSite=strict blocks the cookie on cross-site requests but OWASP treats it as defence in depth, not a replacement for that token
401 versus 403 is not cosmetic. 401 means "I do not know who you are". 403 means valid credentials that are not sufficient, such as a student hitting a faculty route
Live test: edit one character of the cookie in DevTools and watch the same request turn into a 401

card.h1: Logout, expiry, and the one limit we cannot design away
card.p: Four decisions worth defending in the viva, and the honest gap at the end of them.

ul.li: Cookie, not localStorage. Anything in localStorage is readable by injected script. An httpOnly cookie is not, though XSS still defeats CSRF defences, so it buys containment rather than immunity
The secret lives in .env, gitignored, with a committed .env.example. A string literal in app.js would be in the Git history forever
The login route is rate limited. express-rate-limit caps attempts per IP inside a fixed windowMs and returns 429 past the limit
Logout: POST /api/auth/logout calls res.clearCookie("token") with the same attributes. That removes the browser's copy, which is all a server can do to a cookie

Still open, and we know it: a signed token stays valid until exp, so a copy taken before logout still verifies for the rest of those 15 minutes. Closing that needs short-lived access tokens with refresh rotation, or a jti denylist checked on every request, which reintroduces the server-side state JWTs were chosen to avoid

brief.instruction: Write for B.Tech students and a lab instructor watching a live demonstration: technically precise, plain, confident, no marketing register. Target about 55 words per slide; the template holds median 53.5, p90 108, so budget 55 and only approach 100 on a deliberately text-only slide. Code, identifiers, HTTP verbs, routes, status codes, cookie attributes and header names must be reproduced exactly as written in the outline. They are the technical content and a typo destroys credibility in front of an instructor. Keep inline code in code formatting so it reads as code on the slide. Vary sentence and paragraph length. One idea per sentence. Never the "Bold term: explanation" rhythm on every single bullet in a row. The outline uses run-in labels deliberately in some places and plain sentences in others; keep that mix. No signposting ("Let's explore", "In this section"), no sweeping openers, no summary or inspirational closer. The last slide ends on the unresolved revocation problem and that is intentional. No "not just X, it's Y" constructions. No em dashes in the slide copy. Do not invent benchmark numbers, timings, user counts, or percentages. Every figure that appears must come from the outline.

Three corrections are load-bearing. Do not let any of them regress. 1. A compact JWT has TWO dots separating THREE parts (header.payload.signature). Never write or draw three dots. Any diagram of the token shows exactly two separators. 2. This deck describes ONE authentication design end to end: the signed JWT is delivered and returned in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite=strict cookie, and the server reads it with cookie-parser as req.cookies.token. There is no Authorization header and no Bearer token anywhere in this deck, in copy or in any request/response card, diagram or mockup. Because the credential is now sent automatically by the browser, the CSRF point on slide 6 must stay; do not present SameSite alone as complete CSRF protection. 3. No source code was supplied for this portal. Present it as a proposed reference implementation for the lab, as slide 3 states. Do not invent a history of bugs, earlier broken versions, incidents, or "what we got wrong first". Slide 7 is a set of design decisions with one honest unresolved limit, not a postmortem. Separate the three registers where it matters. Facts carry citations and come from the cited sources. Illustrative values chosen for the lab (cost 12, 15-minute expiry, the example hash and roll numbers, the student name on the cover) are our own choices, not recommendations from any source. Interpretation, such as calling bcrypt the knowing legacy choice or containment rather than immunity, is our judgement and should read as judgement.

Premium dark developer-dashboard aesthetic throughout: near-black ground, frosted glassmorphic panels with soft edges, restrained neon glow on accents only, monospace for code, identifiers, routes and metadata labels. Cool cyan/violet readout ink with one warm signal colour reserved for the element that matters on each slide (the accent bar, the failing branch, the changed value). Keep it premium and quiet, never a "hacker" cliche: no matrix rain, no green-on-black terminal spam, no padlock clipart. Per-slide visual intent: Slide 1 (cover): full-bleed dark hero with subtle glow, title lower-left over a deliberately dark quiet region. Slide 2: security-shield visual paired with a contrast between a fast hash and a slow adaptive hash. The bcrypt-as-legacy-option nuance is the point, so do not let the visual imply bcrypt is the recommended best choice. Slide 3: the deck's centrepiece. 3D/isometric software-architecture diagram of the three tiers with clear directional data-flow arrows, the trust boundary marked between browser and API. Give this slide room. Slide 4: realistic browser UI mockup of the registration form beside an API request/response card pair, plus an exploded, labelled breakdown of the 60-character bcrypt string. The four segment labels must line up with the segments they name. Slide 5: paired request/response cards for success and failure. Show the Set-Cookie response header legibly, since it is the slide's technical payload. Render the JWT as three visually distinct segments joined by exactly two dot separators. Slide 6: directional flow diagram of the middleware gate with the 401 and 403 branches visibly breaking away from the happy path; a shield motif on the gate itself. The incoming request carries a cookie, not an Authorization header. Slide 7: quieter card. Treat the four decisions as decisions rather than before-and-after fixes, and leave the final unresolved item visually open rather than ticked off. The template's house rule says to signal direction with words rather than arrows. Override it: the user explicitly asked for clear directional data-flow arrows, and slides 3 and 6 must have them. Every code snippet shown must be legible at projection distance from the back of a lab. Legibility beats fitting more lines; if a snippet will not fit, shorten the snippet rather than shrinking the type.
Exactly 7 slides. This is a hard constraint from the user. Do not add an agenda slide, a divider, a thank-you slide, or a sources slide.
